Health and Environmental Control recommended that no more than 1.5 pounds of fish flesh from Lake Jocassee be eaten per week. Continued sampling will be necessary to determine if mercury levels continue to decline in Jocassee fish.
Aquatic Biota
Lake Jocassee contains a diverse assemblage of forage, nonpredatory, and predatory fishes that occupy a variety of habitats. A list of fishes known to inhabit Lake Jocassee is found in Appendix C. Indigenous species and those established from past introductions into the Upper Savannah River system and now found in Lake Jocassee have been supplemented by stocking programs.
Fish population surveys conducted in Lake Jocassee are reported by Archer (1973). Data for 1972 indicate an immature, primarily warmwater gamefish community. Generally few fish were of harvestable size. Standing crops were high but 80 to 90 percent of the samples were intermediate-sized crappie (Pomoxis sp.) of poor condition. Other observations, based on the 1972 Lake Jocassee sampling, indicated a bluegill (Lepomis macrochirus) population in better condition and a largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides) population in poorer condition relative to results of population surveys conducted at Lake Keowee (Archer, 1974). Lake Jocassee was about 50 feet below full pool during the sampling period.
For 1973, Archer (1974) reported that the Lake Jocassee fish populations approached maturity with 90 percent of the fish of harvestable size. Standing crops declined significantly from the 1972 sampling, but size distribution improved. Largemouth bass averaged less than one pound and were in marginal condition. Large numbers of stunted crappie (Pomoxis sp.) dominated the gamefish samples and were of good size and in good condition. Lake Jocassee was about 20 feet below full pool elevation during the sampling period.
The results of cove rotenone sampling in Lake Jocassee revealed an average production (pooled samples) of 136 pounds per acre in 1972, 75 pounds per acre in 1973, 18 pounds per acre in 1974, and 25 pounds per acre in 1975 (Talbot, 1974). While threadfish shad increased substantially in the latter two years over levels found in 1973 and 1974, no trout were reported for any cf the rotenone samples. Largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides) also appear to be increasing after a sharp drop in 1973.
